title: Word Search
statement:
A word-puzzle app shows a grid of letters. A player traces a word by starting on any cell and moving one cell up, down, left or right for each next letter. Diagonal moves are not allowed, and a single trace may not use the same cell twice.

The grid board is a list of strings of equal length; board[r][c] is row r, column c. Write def solution(board, word) that returns True if word can be traced on the grid and False if not.

examples.why: The LeetCode 79 example 1. A, B, C along the top row, then C, E, D.
The LeetCode 79 example 2. Start at the S on the right edge, go down to E, then left to E.
The LeetCode 79 example 3. A, B, C can be traced, but the B next to that C is already used.

constraints: the board and the word use uppercase and lowercase English letters; case matters

think.a: A sequence of len(word) cells where cell i holds word[i], each cell shares a side with the one before, and no cell appears twice. You only need to say whether one exists, so you can stop at the first success.

S appears at (1, 0) and (1, 3). From (1, 0) the neighbours are A, F, A: no E, dead end. From (1, 3): up is E at (0, 3). From (0, 3) the only other neighbour is C at (0, 2): dead end, so back up. Down from (1, 3) is E at (2, 3), and its left neighbour (2, 2) is E. Found: (1, 3), (2, 3), (2, 2). The 'back up and try the next direction' step is the backtracking.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: From every cell, list every path of len(word) distinct, side-touching cells, and compare the letters on it to the word. It is correct, but it keeps extending paths whose first letter is already wrong: up to cells x 4 x 3^(L - 1) paths for a word of length L.

Backtracking (DFS with undo). Extend a path one letter at a time and stop the moment a cell does not match the next letter. Mark a cell as used before you go deeper and unmark it when you come back, so other paths can use it. The worst case is still exponential, but mismatches cut most branches at once. A cheap extra check: if the board has fewer copies of some letter than the word needs, return False before searching.

1. If some letter appears in word more often than on the board, return False.
  2. Copy the board into a list of lists so you can mark cells.
  3. dfs(r, c, i): if the cell is not word[i], return False. If i is the last index, return True. Mark the cell '#', try the 4 neighbours with i + 1, restore the letter, and return whether any neighbour succeeded.
  4. Try dfs(r, c, 0) from every cell; return True on the first success.
The recursion is at most len(word) deep, at most 15.

A word that needs a cell twice ("ABCB" in example 3). A one-letter word. A word longer than the number of cells. A 1 x 1 board. A path that must turn back up or left. Upper and lower case. Forgetting to unmark a cell on the way back, which wrongly blocks later paths.

hints: Try every cell as the start. From a matching cell, the next letter must be in one of its 4 neighbours.
Walk the path one letter at a time and give up on a branch as soon as a letter does not match. A cell on the current path may not be used again.
Mark the cell (for example with '#') before exploring its neighbours and put its letter back afterwards. Return as soon as the last index matches.
explain:
Example 1, word = "ABCCED" on ["ABCE", "SFCS", "ADEE"]:

  • Start at (0, 0), which is A. Mark it. Up and left are outside; down is S, not B; right is B at (0, 1).
  • From B: right is C at (0, 2). From that C: right is E, not C; down is C at (1, 2).
  • From (1, 2): down is E at (2, 2). From there, left is D at (2, 1): the last letter. Return True.

Example 3, "ABCB", reaches A, B, C the same way, but the only B next to that C is (0, 1), which is marked as used. Every other branch fails on its first letter, so the answer is False. Marking before going deeper and restoring after is what lets a cell be skipped on this path yet used by the next one.
complexity: O(rows x cols x 3^L) time in the worst case for a word of length L (4 directions at the first step, 3 after); O(L) recursion depth
